extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American government and politics (college-level)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook chapter describing the organization and administration of the U.S. military (War and Navy Departments), conduct of war, citizens' rights in wartime, pension administration, and constitutional rules and practices governing taxation and revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War, appointed by the President and Senate, directs the military establishments of the United States; he has charge of the fortifications, river and harbor improvements, and bridges; he supervises the administration of the Philippine Islands, the construction of the Panama Canal, and the government of the Canal Zone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He must subject to examination all estimates of appropriations for the expenses of his department and the entire military establishment, including the purchase of military supplies; scrutinize expenditures for support, transportation, and maintenance of the army; and oversee other expenditures placed in his charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assistant Secretary of War responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: A great portion of the Secretary's heavy burden is directly assigned by law to an assistant secretary of war, who has charge of many matters—rivers and harbors, bridges over navigable waters, the recruiting service, courts martial, the militia, etc., and the preliminary questions relating to Cuba and the Philippines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine and numerous specific duties are vested in this office to relieve the Secretary; other routine duties are vested in a chief clerk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjutant-General duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The adjutant-general records, authenticates, and transmits to the troops and individuals the orders, instructions, and regulations which go out from the central administration; he also has general charge of the records and statistics of the army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions as central administrative record-keeper and distributor of orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspector-General duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The inspector-general supervises the inspection of the army in all of its branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides oversight of military readiness and conduct through inspections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartermaster-General duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The quartermaster-general and his assistants have charge of transportation, buildings, and supplies, including the purchase and distribution of rations, the payment of the officers and men, in short almost all equipment except munitions of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsible for logistical support and material readiness of the army (excluding ordnance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgeon-General duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The surgeon-general supervises the medical department of the army and gives special attention to sanitary affairs which are of such great importance in war and peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oversees medical services and public health/sanitation matters for the military.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief of Engineers duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief of engineers is at the head of the corps of engineers which looks after the construction and maintenance of forts, military roads, and bridges, and river and harbor improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads engineering projects critical to military infrastructure and civil-military works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordnance Department responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordnance department, which provides and distributes the implements of war, is in charge of the chief of ordnance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsible for munitions, weapons, and related ordnance supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief Signal Officer responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The means of communication throughout all branches of the army are under the scrutiny of the chief signal officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures communication infrastructure and protocols across military branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge-Advocate-General (Army) duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge-advocate-general is directed by law to receive, review, and have recorded the proceedings of all courts-martial, courts of inquiry, and military commissions; and it is also his duty to give the Secretary of War information and advice on legal questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts as legal officer for military justice and legal counsel to the Secretary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureau of Insular Affairs role
rubrics_metrics.description: The general supervision of the administration on the Philippine Islands is vested in the chief of the bureau of insular affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handles administration and oversight of U.S. insular possessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Staff composition and term limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress created a General Staff to be composed of officers detailed from the army at large under rules prescribed by the President. Officers detailed to the General Staff may serve in that capacity for only four years at most; and on returning to the army they must remain there at least two years before they can be detailed again, except in time of emergency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff includes general officers and lower ranks to maintain contact with rank-and-file; term limits designed to keep staff in touch with practical problems of warfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief of the General Staff / Chief of Staff role
rubrics_metrics.description: The head of the staff is the Chief of the Staff, who acts under the direction of the President and the Secretary of War. The office of the Chief of Staff constitutes, for administrative purposes, a supervising military bureau in the War Department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions as principal military advisor and administrative head of the General Staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Staff functions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of the General Staff to prepare plans for national defence and for the mobilization of the national forces in time of war; to investigate and report upon all questions relating to the efficiency of the army and its state of preparation; to render professional aid to the Secretary of War and to the general officers and their superior commanders; and perform such other military duties, not otherwise assigned by law, as the President may from time to time prescribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides planning, evaluation, professional military advice, and other duties assigned by the President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of the Navy duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of the Navy, appointed by the President and Senate, is authorized to perform such duties as the President may assign him, and to superintend the construction, manning, armament, equipment, and employment of vessels of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by assistant secretary and chief clerk; oversees all naval administration and readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Navy Department bureau structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The administration of the Navy Department is distributed among the following bureaus, the general administrative duties of each of which are made clear by the titles: navigation, yards and docks, ordnance, construction and repair, steam engineering, medicine and surgery, and supplies and accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel bureau structure to War Department for specialized naval functions; includes judge-advocate-general and commandant of the marine corps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military and Naval Academy appointment and commissioning rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Military Academy at West Point and the Naval Academy at Annapolis maintain cadet quotas by assigning appointments to Senators, Representatives, Delegates, the District of Columbia, and the President; nominees must pass examinations testing preparation for the course; cadets who complete West Point are commissioned as second lieutenants; midshipmen on passing graduation are assigned to rank in the lower ranges of the naval service on a basis of their merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cadet/midshipman appointments are geographically apportioned, require entrance examinations, and graduates receive commissioning/advantage in active service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment and removal of army and navy officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Army and navy officers are appointed by the President and Senate. In time of peace army and navy officers may be removed only by court-martial; but in time of war the President may remove summarily. Provision is also made by law for retirement and promotion subject to a certain presidential discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiates peacetime legal protections from wartime executive flexibility; retirement/promotion governed by law with presidential discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: President as commander-in-chief powers
rubrics_metrics.description: As commander-in-chief he may dispose of the armed forces on land and sea in time of war and peace; he may supervise the execution of the military law in the government of the troops; and, when Congress has declared war, or the United States has been invaded, he may employ the soldiers and direct their operations, subject to the rules of that branch of international law known as the law of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive war powers include operational command and legal supervision of military forces, constrained by law of war and influenced by practical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct of war: division of responsibility and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The President and his immediate advisers in Washington sketch the general plans of campaign; supervise their execution; make changes and issue new directions from time to time, cooperating with the officers at the front, trusting more or less to their use of discretion amid the exigencies of battle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent of presidential control depends on theatre, communication, the President's military ability, and regard for subordinate officers; General Staff provides expert advice closely in touch with the army.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of citizens in time of war / martial law limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of American citizens must be determined according to the Constitution. Ex parte Milligan held that in time of civil war when courts are actually closed by foreign invasion and it is impossible to administer criminal justice according to law, the military authority has the right to rule by martial law until the laws can have free course again; but martial rule can never be maintained where the courts are open and in the proper and undisturbed exercise of their jurisdiction, and it is confined to the locality of actual war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raises issues such as arrest of citizens in loyal states, suspension of habeas corpus, jury trial for military arrests; doctrine includes that necessity creates the rule but also limits its duration—practical presidential control may nonetheless be broad in wartime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pension system principles and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States has been liberal in the provision of pensions for soldiers and sailors and those dependent upon them; following every war there is a new series of pension laws, making provision for those who have served; many widows, children under sixteen, and helpless minors are provided for, and state and national homes are established for the disabled and indigent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administration of the pensions is in charge of a commissioner in the Department of the Interior; laws may change basis (e.g., May 11, 1912 provision for pensioning veterans of Mexican and Civil Wars on basis of term of service rather than disabilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal cost of war and implication for spending priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: A large portion of federal revenues is expended for army, navy, fortifications, pensions, interest, and other charges incurred by past wars; examples given (fiscal year 1908 figures and percentages) illustrate that a high percentage of revenue may be devoted to military purposes and past-war charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text records arguments that high military spending (e.g., 72% of revenue in one cited accounting) should prompt public attention and debate over allocations and international arrangements to limit armaments; defenders argue necessity to protect possessions and commerce and to avoid past mistakes of neglecting military preparedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional taxing power (general pronouncement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Constitution Congress has a general power to lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts, and excises. Subject to certain rules, there is no limit on the amount of taxes Congress may lay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief Justice quoted that if the power to tax is exercised oppressively the remedy rests with the people who choose the legislature; taxing power must be exercised according to due process of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity requirement for duties, imposts, and excises
rubrics_metrics.description: It is provided in the Constitution that all duties, imposts, and excises shall be uniform throughout the United States; under Supreme Court interpretation a uniform tax is one which falls with the same weight upon the same object wherever found within the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: passenger duty held uniform though levied principally at a few ports; inheritance tax uniform when imposed equally on all inheritances of the same amount and character even if taxable inheritances occur in only a few states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment requirement for direct taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct taxes (except income taxes prior to amendment) shall be apportioned among the states according to their respective numbers (population).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically direct taxes were capitation/poll and land taxes; Supreme Court in 1895 held taxes upon income from real and personal property were direct and therefore constitutional only when apportioned. Due to difficulty and injustice of apportionment, the constitutional limitation was effectively prohibitive until the Sixteenth Amendment (1913) authorized income taxes without apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on taxing exports and preference between states
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution provides that Congress shall not lay a duty or tax on articles exported from any state, and that in the regulation of commerce and revenue no preference shall be given to the ports of one state over those of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent discrimination between states it is further stipulated that vessels bound to or from one state shall not be obliged to enter, clear, or pay duties in the ports of another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied constitutional restriction: immunity of state instrumentalities
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to express limitations there is an important implied restriction on the taxing power: Congress cannot tax the instrumentalities or the property of any state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in cases (e.g., during Civil War an income tax was held inapplicable to income derived from a commonwealth); doctrine traces to cases such as McCulloch v. Maryland as source of state immunity principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between direct and indirect taxes (categories and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly speaking there are two forms of taxes in the United States, direct and indirect. Direct taxes historically included capitation (poll) and taxes on land; indirect taxes include excise taxes upon commodities (whiskey, tobacco), customs duties on imports, taxes upon inheritances, license taxes on occupations, stamp taxes on commercial transactions, and taxes on incomes not derived from real or personal property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court caselaw has varied (e.g., Springer held some income taxes indirect; later holdings treated some income taxes as direct). Classification determines whether apportionment or uniformity rule applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue practice: reliance on indirect taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in time of war or shortage of revenue it has been the general practice of the federal government to rely upon indirect taxation as its prime source of revenue. The Fathers intended that indirect taxes should be the chief resort of the central government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect taxes are preferred because of public dislike of lump-sum direct taxes and because indirect taxes are administratively simpler (falling in small amounts upon consumer articles and imposed uniformly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixteenth Amendment effect and early income-tax practice (1913 law features)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1913, after long agitation, a constitutional amendment (Sixteenth Amendment) was adopted authorizing Congress to lay taxes upon private incomes from all sources without apportionment. The 1913 tax imposed one per cent upon private incomes above $3000 with increasing rates on incomes over $20,000, with certain exemptions; any person supporting a wife or husband is allowed a $4000 exemption, and incomes from government bonds (federal, state, and local) are exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marks a major departure from near-complete reliance on customs and excises; earlier (1909) corporate income tax and 1913 personal income tax broadened revenue sources.
